Jakarta Persistence

This book models how construction and lifecycle operations affect an entity's state and persistent identity in one persistence context. Sections 2.1 and 2.4 introduce entity instances and identity. Selected parts of section 3.6 pair the lifecycle rules with checked Lean/Veil code. The proofs, finite regression checks, and proof trust audit follow.

Formalized Specification

The numbered sections are excerpts from Jakarta Persistence 4.0-M4 (May 25, 2026, DRAFT), authored by the Jakarta Persistence Team. Each excerpt keeps its original section number. Blocks labelled Formalized Specification contain the project's explanations and checked Lean code.

2. Entities🔗

2.1. The Entity Class🔗

The entity class must be annotated with the Entity annotation or declared as an entity in its XML descriptor.

  • The entity class must be a top-level class or a static inner class. An enum, record, or interface may not be designated as an entity.

  • The entity class must have a public or protected constructor with no parameters, which is called by the persistence provider runtime to instantiate the entity.[2] This constructor is usually declared in the Java source code, but it might be added using source or bytecode processing by the build process or runtime environment.[3] The entity class may have additional constructors for use by the application.

  • The entity class must be non-final. Every method and persistent instance variable of the entity class must also be non-final.

An entity might be an abstract class, or it might be a concrete class. An entity may extend a non-entity class, or it may extend another entity class. A non-entity class may extend an entity class.

The persistent state of an entity is represented by instance variables, which may correspond to JavaBeans properties. An instance variable may be directly accessed only within the methods of the entity, by the entity instance itself. An instance variable of an entity must not be directly accessed by a client of the entity. The state of the entity is available to clients only through the methods of the entity—​that is, via accessor (getter/setter) methods, or via other business methods.

2. The term "persistence provider runtime" refers to the runtime environment of the persistence implementation. In a JakartaEE environment, this might be the Jakarta EE container itself, or a third-party persistence provider implementation integrated with the container.

3. When the constructor is added by tooling or by the container, the entity source code is not portable to environments where such tooling is unavailable.

Formalized Specification

An entity class describes a kind of Java object; an entity instance is an individual object of that class. For example, suppose that both Person and Employee are entity classes and Employee extends Person. Creating two Employee objects produces two instances of the same entity class.

Our lifecycle model represents individual instances. It assumes they belong to valid entity classes; it does not check annotations, constructors, or the other class requirements above.

We use Veil, a modeling language embedded in Lean, to declare the model and its operations. The following command opens a module named EntityLifecycle.

veil module EntityLifecycle

The type entity represents individual Java objects, the instances discussed in section 2.1. Each value identifies one possible object. The model does not record its class or fields.

type entity

2.4. Primary Keys and Entity Identity🔗

Every entity must have a primary key. The value of its primary key uniquely identifies an entity instance within a persistence context and to operations of the EntityManager or EntityAgent, as described in Chapter 3, and represents the persistent identity of the instance, a concept which is defined more carefully later in Section 3.6.10.

The primary key must be declared by:

  • the entity class that is the root of the entity hierarchy, or

  • a mapped superclass that is a (direct or indirect) superclass of all entity classes in the entity hierarchy.

A primary key must be defined exactly once in each entity hierarchy.

Note

Terminology Note: In the community, the primary key of an entity is usually called its identifier, but for historical reasons that term is not used in this specification.

A primary key comprises one or more fields or properties (attributes) of the entity class.

  • A simple primary key is a single persistent field or property of the entity class whose type is one of the legal simple primary key types listed below. The Id annotation defined in Section 11.2.24 or id XML element must be used to identify the simple primary key.

  • A composite primary key may be declared as either a single persistent field or property, or as a set of fields or properties, as described below.[11] A primary key class must be defined to represent the composite primary key.

    • If the composite primary key is represented by a single field or property of the entity, the EmbeddedId annotation defined by Section 11.2.18 identifies the primary key, and the type of the annotated field or property is the primary key class.

    • Otherwise, when the composite primary key encompasses multiple fields or properties, the Id annotation defined by Section 11.2.24 identifies the fields and properties which belong to the composite key, and the IdClass annotation defined by Section 11.2.25 must specify the primary key class.

A simple primary key or a field or property belonging to a composite primary key must have one of the following basic types:

  • any Java primitive type, or java.lang wrapper for a primitive type, [12]

  • java.lang.String,

  • java.util.UUID,

  • java.time.LocalDate, java.util.Date, or java.sql.Date,

  • BigDecimal or BigInteger from java.math.

If a primary key field or property has type java.util.Date, the temporal type must be explicitly specified as DATE using the Temporal annotation defined by Section 11.2.56, or by equivalent XML.

If the primary key is a composite primary key derived from the primary key of another entity, the primary key may contain an attribute whose type is that of the primary key of the referenced entity, as specified below in Section 2.4.2.

An entity with a primary key involving any type other than the types listed above is not portable. If the primary key is generated by the persistence provider, as defined by Section 11.2.23, and its type is not long, int, java.util.UUID, java.lang.String, java.lang.Long, or java.lang.Integer, the entity is not portable.

The application must not change the value of the primary key of an entity instance after the instance is made persistent[13]. If the application does change the value of a primary key of an entity instance after the entity instance is made persistent, the behavior is undefined.[14]

11. Composite primary keys often arise when mapping a legacy database with primary keys comprising multiple columns.

12. Although tolerated by Jakarta Persistence, approximate numeric types (floating point types) should never be used in primary keys.

13. This includes not changing the value of a mutable type that is primary key or an attribute of a composite primary key.

14. The implementation may, but is not required to, throw an exception. Portable applications must not rely on any such specific behavior.

Formalized Specification

Object identity tells us whether two references point to the same Java object. Persistent identity tells us which persistent entity an object represents. The root entity class is the highest entity class in the inheritance hierarchy. Section 3.6.10 defines persistent identity as the pair consisting of that class and the primary-key value.

In the example from section 2.1, suppose Person is the root entity class. An Employee with primary key 7 has persistent identity (Person, 7). If Book is another root entity class, a book with key 7 has a different persistent identity, (Book, 7). Conversely, a detached Employee and the managed copy returned by merge can be distinct Java objects with the same persistent identity.

The model uses the abstract type identity to compare persistent identities. Its declaration gives no access to the class or key separately. The type also includes noIdentity, introduced in section 3.6 to represent the absence of a persistent identity.

type identity

3. Entity Operations🔗

3.6. Entity Instance Lifecycle🔗

Any entity instance can be characterized as being in one of the following lifecycle states with respect to a given persistence context:

  • A new entity instance has no persistent identity and is not yet associated with any persistence context.

  • A managed entity instance is an instance with a persistent identity that is currently associated with a persistence context.

  • A detached entity instance is an instance with a persistent identity that is not (or no longer) associated with a persistence context.

  • A removed entity instance is an instance with a persistent identity, and associated with a persistence context, that is scheduled for removal from the database upon transaction commit.

Certain operations of EntityManager modify the lifecycle state of an entity instance. The following subsections describe the effect of such lifecycle operations.

Formalized Specification

With entity instances and persistent identities defined in Chapter 2, we now describe their lifecycle states and operations within one persistence context.

The four lifecycle states defined above become an enumeration:

enum phase = {new, managed, detached, removed}

We use noIdentity to represent the absence of a persistent identity. In Veil, individual declares a single named value of the specified type, and immutable means that operations cannot change that value.

immutable individual noIdentity : identity

To check the lifecycle of the entities, we now define a relation and a function. The first one, created, tracks whether an instance has been constructed, whether or not it is attached to a persistence context. A newly constructed instance is transient, but created remains true when it becomes managed or detached. The function e_phase instead tracks the phase the instance is in.

You might wonder why e_phase e = new is not enough and why we also need to track whether the instance has been constructed.

That's because new is the initial value of e_phase e, and the model includes identifiers for possible instances that haven't yet been constructed. So we must define how e_phase e behaves even when the object represented by e doesn't exist yet, that is, when created e = false. In that case, new is only a placeholder.

For each entity instance, we define a created relation to state whether it has been constructed. “Relation” here is a mathematical term used in proof assistants such as Lean. It does not mean a JPA relationship. A relation records a true-or-false fact for its arguments. In Lean, predicates commonly return Prop. Veil's stored relations return Bool so their values can be computed when executing the model checker. Here, entity → Bool means that each entity has a Boolean value, which operations can update.

relation created : entity → Bool

The function e_phase records each instance's lifecycle state.

function e_phase : entity → phase

The function pid records each instance's persistent identity, or noIdentity if it has none.

function pid : entity → identity

With these declarations in place, #gen_state generates the Lean type that holds the model's state.

#gen_state

So far, we have introduced the type identity and named one value of that type, noIdentity, to represent the absence of a persistent identity. We have not yet required the type to contain any other values. If noIdentity were its only value, the persist operation could never assign a persistent identity to a new instance.

We therefore assume that the same type contains at least one other value that can represent a persistent identity.

assumption [nonempty_identities] ∃ i, i ≠ noIdentity

To express the specification's requirements and reason about them in the following proofs, we introduce names for three conditions on the model's state:

  • belongsToContext e: instance e belongs to the persistence context represented by this model.

  • pendingRemoval e: instance e is marked for database deletion.

  • identityAvailable i means identity i is available to assign to an instance.

These conditions are defined using the information we already record: which instances have been constructed, their lifecycle states, and their persistent identities. Veil calls these definitions ghost relations: they give us vocabulary for describing and reasoning about the state without adding independently stored information.

The model describes one fixed persistence context. Each instance's lifecycle state is interpreted relative to that context. Constructing an instance leaves it in the new state, outside the context. Successfully persisting that instance changes its state to managed, establishing its association with the context.

The condition belongsToContext e holds when e has been constructed and its lifecycle state is either managed or removed. The check created e only establishes that the object has been constructed; it says nothing about who constructed it. The removed state means marked for database deletion while still associated with the context, as defined in the specification above. This membership condition therefore differs from EntityManager.contains(), which excludes removed instances.

When an operation changes e_phase e to detached, the membership condition is no longer satisfied, so belongsToContext e is false. We use this condition in the identity uniqueness requirement and the merge operation.

ghost relation belongsToContext (e : entity) := created e ∧ (e_phase e = managed ∨ e_phase e = removed)

The condition pendingRemoval e holds when instance e has been constructed and its lifecycle state is removed. It describes scheduled database deletion; the model does not represent the deletion itself.

ghost relation pendingRemoval (e : entity) := created e ∧ e_phase e = removed

The condition identityAvailable i holds when i is an actual persistent identity and no constructed instance has that identity. This includes checking detached instances, even though they are outside the context. We exclude noIdentity because it represents the absence of an identity. For every instance e, if it has been constructed, its identity must differ from i.

ghost relation identityAvailable (i : identity) := i ≠ noIdentity ∧ ∀ e, created e → pid e ≠ i

Initially, no instances have been constructed. We give every possible instance the default lifecycle state new and the identity value noIdentity. The after_init block establishes these initial values. Here the uppercase variable E makes each assignment apply to every entity, and := assigns a value.

after_init { created E := false e_phase E := new pid E := noIdentity }

3.6.1. Lifecycle Operations🔗

The fundamental operations of an EntityManager are:

  • persist() to make a new entity persistent, as defined in Section 3.6.3,

  • remove(), to remove a persistent entity from the database, as defined in Section 3.6.4,

  • flush(), to force synchronization of pending modifications with the database, as defined in Section 3.6.6,

  • refresh(), to reload an entity from the database, as defined in Section 3.6.7,

  • detach(), to disassociate an entity from its persistence context, as defined in Section 3.6.8,

  • merge(), to copy the state of a detached instance into the persistence context, and

  • lock() to obtain a lock an entity instance or to upgrade the lock level currently held, as defined in Section 3.9.

The methods persist(), remove(), refresh(), detach(), and merge() are called lifecycle operations.

The cascade annotation element of a relationship modeling annotation, as defined in Section 2.11, specifies which lifecycle operations propagate to associated entities. Each lifecycle operation is identified by the corresponding member of the enumeration CascadeType.

public enum CascadeType {ALL, PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH}

The value cascade=ALL is equivalent to cascade={PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH}.

Note

The cascade functionality is most typically used to model parent-child relationships. A closely related feature is orphan removal, which is defined below in Section 3.6.5.

Information about how lifecycle operations interact with transactions may be found below in Section 3.7.2.

3.6.2. Entity Instance Creation🔗

An instance of an entity class may be created using the new operator. A newly instantiated instance is not considered persistent—​that is, it is not considered to represent a record in the database—​and the new instance is not associated with a persistence context. A new instance is not considered to have a well-defined persistent identity until it is made persistent.

Formalized Specification

You can't create already created entities

action Create (e : entity) { require ¬ created e created e := true assert ¬ belongsToContext e assert pid e = noIdentity }

3.6.3. Persisting an Entity Instance🔗

A new instance becomes persistent when it is passed as an argument to the persist() method of EntityManager or when the persist operation cascades from another instance to the new instance.

Let e be an instance of an entity class. If e is passed as an argument to the persist() method of EntityManager, or if the persist operation is applied to e via cascade:

  • if e is a new entity, it becomes managed and a new record represented by e will be inserted into the database at or before transaction commit as a result of the flush operation specified below in Section 3.6.6;

  • if e is a managed entity already associated with the persistence context, e itself is ignored by the persist operation;

  • if e is a removed entity, it becomes managed; or

  • if e is a detached entity, either an EntityExistsException is thrown immediately, or an EntityExistsException or some other subtype of PersistenceException is thrown when the persistence context is flushed or when the transaction commits.

  • If e is new, managed, or removed, the persist operation is also applied to every entity t referenced by a relationship owned by e and annotated with the cascade element value cascade=PERSIST or cascade=ALL or mapped as such by the equivalent XML descriptor element.

Ordinarily, the persist operation assigns a persistent identity to the entity. If the primary key of the entity is a generated value, as defined by Section 11.2.23, the primary key is generated as part of the persist operation, and the generated value is made available to the application by setting the primary key field or property of the entity. As a special exception to this rule, if the primary key generation strategy of an entity is IDENTITY, the persistence provider is permitted to delay assignment of the primary key until pending modifications are synchronized with the database, as defined by Section 3.6.6. Indeed, when persist() is called with no active transaction, the persistence provider is required to delay generation and assignment of IDENTITY primary keys.

Formalized Specification

Persist requires a created instance whose lifecycle state is new, managed, or removed. The two require conditions below exclude instances that have not been constructed and calls on detached instances.

For a new instance, let i : identity :| identityAvailable i chooses an available identity. The symbol :| introduces the condition on that choice. Any identity satisfying it is allowed, and the proofs must cover every such choice. The action assigns this identity and makes the instance managed.

For a removed instance, the action changes its state back to managed, cancelling its pending removal. For an already managed instance, neither branch applies, so the modeled state remains unchanged.

action Persist (e : entity) { require created e require e_phase e ≠ detached if e_phase e = new then let i : identity :| identityAvailable i pid e := i e_phase e := managed else if e_phase e = removed then e_phase e := managed }

Identity assignment and the change to managed happen in one model step. This simplifies the specification's rules for delayed IDENTITY assignment. Assigned identities are never released for reuse in this model. In a finite model, persisting a new instance becomes impossible when no identity is available. This limit does not represent a JPA exception.

3.6.4. Removal🔗

A managed entity instance becomes removed when it is passed as an argument to the remove() method of EntityManager or when the remove operation cascades from another instance to the managed instance.

Let e be an instance of an entity class. If e is passed as an argument to the remove() method of EntityManager, or if the remove operation is applied to e via cascade:

  • if e is a new entity, e itself is ignored by the remove operation;

  • if e is a managed entity, it is marked as removed and the record represented by e is scheduled for deletion from the database at or before transaction commit as a result of the flush operation specified below in Section 3.6.6;

  • if e is a removed entity, e itself is ignored by the remove operation; or

  • if e is a detached entity, an IllegalArgumentException is thrown or a failure occurs later when the flush operation occurs.

  • If e is new, managed, or removed, the remove operation is also applied to every entity t referenced by a relationship owned by e and annotated with the cascade element value cascade=REMOVE or cascade=ALL or mapped as such by the equivalent XML descriptor element.

The remove() method does not change the state held by fields of the entity instance itself.

Formalized Specification

Remove requires a created instance that is not detached. It changes a managed instance's lifecycle state to removed. For new or already removed instances, it leaves the state unchanged.

action Remove (e : entity) { require created e require e_phase e ≠ detached if e_phase e = managed then e_phase e := removed }

The action does not change the instance's persistent identity. Since belongsToContext includes removed instances, it also preserves context membership. The definition pendingRemoval becomes true when a managed instance is removed; deletion of a database record is outside the model.

3.6.7. Refreshing an Entity Instance🔗

The state of a managed entity instance is refreshed from the database when it is passed as an argument to the refresh() method of EntityManager or when the refresh operation cascades from another instance to the managed instance.

Let e be an instance of an entity class. If e is passed as the first argument to the refresh() method of EntityManager, or if the refresh operation is applied to e via cascade:

  • if e is a managed entity, the state of e is refreshed from the database by reading the record represented by e and modifying the state of e to match, overwriting any pending modifications made to the entity; or

  • if e is a new, detached, or removed entity, the IllegalArgumentException is thrown.

  • If e is managed, the refresh operation is also applied to every entity t referenced by a relationship owned by e and annotated with the cascade element value cascade=REFRESH or cascade=ALL or mapped as such by the equivalent XML descriptor element.

Formalized Specification

Only a managed entity may successfully refresh. Refresh reloads fields from the database, but neither fields nor database contents are part of our state. The action therefore leaves the modeled state unchanged.

Its only requirement is that the instance exists and is managed. With no assignments in the body, this is an allowed step that preserves every value.

action Refresh (e : entity) { require created e ∧ e_phase e = managed }

3.6.8. Evicting an Entity Instance from the Persistence Context🔗

A managed entity instance is removed from the persistence context when it is passed as an argument to the detach() method of EntityManager or when the detach operation cascades from another instance to the managed instance.

Let e be an instance of an entity class. If e is passed as an argument to the detach() method of EntityManager, or if the detach operation is applied to e via cascade:

  • if e is a managed entity, it is removed from the persistence context and becomes detached;

  • if e is a new or detached entity, it is ignored by the detach operation;

  • if e is a removed entity, it becomes detached, and the scheduled removal of the record represented by e is cancelled.

  • If e is managed or removed, the detach operation is also applied to every entity t referenced by a relationship owned by e and annotated with the cascade element value cascade=DETACH or cascade=ALL or mapped as such by the equivalent XML descriptor element.

Portable applications should not pass removed entities that have been detached from the persistence context to methods of EntityManager.

Entities which referenced e before detachment continue to reference e after detachment.

Note

Pending modifications to the state of the entity, including removal of the entity, are never synchronized to the database after the entity is evicted from the persistence context. If such pending modifications exist, an application must call the flush() method before calling detach() if portable behavior is required. A portable application must not assume that pending modifications have not been written to the database if the flush() method was not called before detach(). More information about synchronization may be found above in Section 3.6.6.

Formalized Specification

Detach requires a created instance. It changes a managed or removed instance to detached and leaves a new or already detached instance unchanged. Its persistent identity is preserved in every case.

action Detach (e : entity) { require created e if e_phase e = managed ∨ e_phase e = removed then e_phase e := detached }

After detachment, both belongsToContext e and pendingRemoval e are false. This represents leaving the context and, for a removed instance, cancelling pending removal. We do not record whether an instance was removed before it was detached, so the model does not enforce the specification's restriction on passing such instances to later EntityManager calls.

3.6.9. Detached Entities🔗

3.6.9.2. Merging Detached Entity State🔗

The merge operation allows for the propagation of state from detached entities to managed instances associated with a persistence context. Given a detached instance, the merge operation returns a managed instance with the same persistent identity and state as the detached instance, but with a distinct Java object identity.

Let e be an instance of an entity class. If e is passed as an argument to the merge() method of EntityManager, or if the merge operation is applied to e via cascade, a merged object e2 is produced:

  • if e is a detached entity, the persistent state of e is copied to a pre-existing managed entity instance e2 of the same identity or, if there is no such pre-existing managed entity, a new managed copy e2 of e is created;

  • if e is a new entity instance, a new managed entity instance e2 is created and the state of e is copied to e2;

  • if e is a removed entity instance, an IllegalArgumentException is thrown or a failure occurs later when the flush operation occurs; or

  • if e is a managed entity, e itself is ignored by the merge operation and the merged object e2 is taken to be identical to e.

  • If e is new, managed, or detached, the merge operation is also applied to every entity t referenced by a relationship owned by e and annotated with the cascade element value cascade=MERGE or cascade=ALL or mapped as such by the equivalent XML descriptor element. For every such t referenced by e, e2 is set to reference the object t2 produced by applying the merge operation to t.

  • For every entity t referenced by e via an association, navigation of the same association from e2 yields a reference to a managed object s with the same persistent identity as t.

If e has a version, as defined in Section 2.5, the persistence provider must validate that e and e2 have the same version, either during processing of the merge operation, or later when the flush operation occurs or when the transaction commits.

The persistence provider must ignore unfetched attributes of detached instances when merging. A persistence provider is permitted to report an exception if an entity instance with unfetched lazy attributes instantiated by a different persistence provider runtime is passed to merge().

Note

When this sort of interoperability across different persistence provider runtimes from different vendors is required, the application must not use lazy loading.

Formalized Specification

Merge involves two instances: the source e and the returned instance target. We include the result as an action argument so that the model can describe which object is returned; the Java method still takes only the source argument. The source must have been created and must not be removed.

For a new source, the target must be an instance that has not yet been created. The action assigns it an available identity and makes it managed. It leaves the source new and without a persistent identity.

For a detached source, an existing target must be managed and have the source's identity. If the target has not been created, the action first checks that no instance in the context has that identity. It then creates a managed target with the source's identity. In both cases, the source stays detached.

For a managed source, the final branch requires target = e: merge returns the source itself and changes nothing. These cases form one action below.

action Merge (e target : entity) { require created e require e_phase e ≠ removed if e_phase e = new then require ¬ created target let i : identity :| identityAvailable i pid target := i created target := true e_phase target := managed else if e_phase e = detached then if created target then require belongsToContext target ∧ e_phase target = managed ∧ pid target = pid e else require ∀ other, belongsToContext other → pid other ≠ pid e created target := true e_phase target := managed pid target := pid e else require target = e }

If a removed instance in the context has a detached source's identity, neither detached branch can succeed: that instance is not a managed target, and its presence prevents creation of another target. We exclude this situation from the successful calls represented by the model.

Creating a managed copy requires an entity value that has not yet been used. Merging a new source also requires an available identity, assigned in the same step. If either required value is unavailable, the action cannot occur. As with construction and persist, this is a model limit, not a JPA exception. Copying fields and checking versions are outside the model.

3.6.10. Managed Entities🔗

It is the responsibility of the persistence provider to ensure that at most one entity instance belonging to a given persistence context has a given persistent identity. The persistent identity of an entity class instance is represented as a pair comprising:

  1. the class of the root entity of the entity class inheritance hierarchy to which the entity class belongs, together with

  2. the value of the primary key of the entity instance, as defined above in Section 2.4.

Therefore, if the entity type X is a subclass of the root entity type Y, and x is an instance of X with primary key k, the persistent identity of x is (Y,k).

It is the responsibility of the application to ensure that an instance of an entity class is associated with at most one persistence context. If an entity instance is made managed in more than one persistence context, the behavior is undefined and unportable.

The contains() method of EntityManager determines whether an entity instance is managed in the associated persistence context. The contains() method returns true if and only if:

  • the argument is a managed entity instance associated with the given persistence context, and

  • the argument entity is not marked as removed.

The effect of cascading persist, merge, remove, or detach is immediately visible to the contains() method, whereas the actual insertion, update, or deletion of the database record represented by the entity is deferred until the flush operation occurs.

Formalized Specification

We now state the conditions that the model must preserve. An invariant is a condition we prove true initially and after every allowed operation. Its name in square brackets identifies the condition in later proofs.

First, an instance is new if and only if it has no persistent identity. The symbol ↔ means “if and only if,” so the condition applies in both directions. The uppercase variable E makes this statement apply to every entity value.

invariant [identityOK] (e_phase E = new ↔ pid E = noIdentity)

An instance that has not been constructed must retain its initial lifecycle state and identity. Once an instance has been created, this condition places no further restriction on it.

invariant [uncreatedOK] ¬ created E → e_phase E = new ∧ pid E = noIdentity

Finally, two instances in the context with the same persistent identity must be the same Java object. We declare this as a safety property: a condition that must hold in every reachable state. Here E and OTHER range over every pair of instances.

safety [uniqueIdentity] belongsToContext E ∧ belongsToContext OTHER ∧ pid E = pid OTHER → E = OTHER

Because belongsToContext includes managed and removed instances, uniqueness applies to both. Detached instances are outside the context and may share an identity with a managed copy.

We prove that the initial state satisfies all three conditions, then show that each operation preserves them whenever they hold before the operation.

The command #gen_spec turns our initialization, actions, and properties into Lean definitions used by the proofs.

#gen_spec

Initially, every instance is new and has noIdentity, so the identity condition holds. The command prove_veil_invariant_goal identifies the initialization or action and the property to prove. The phrase using tr selects its transition relation: the definition of the allowed before-and-after states. After by, we give Lean the proof instructions.

The tactic grind automatically combines the available facts to construct a proof. Lean's kernel checks that proof; we do not accept a solver's answer without a proof.

prove_veil_invariant_goal initializer identityOK using tr by All goals completed! 🐙

Initialization also gives every uncreated instance its required defaults.

prove_veil_invariant_goal initializer uncreatedOK using tr by All goals completed! 🐙

No instance belongs to the context initially, so two context members cannot have conflicting identities.

prove_veil_invariant_goal initializer uniqueIdentity using tr by All goals completed! 🐙

An unconstructed instance starts in phase new with noIdentity, and Create changes only its construction flag. Since only managed and removed instances belong to the context, both assertions in Create hold. The doesNotThrow proof checks this for every construction from a state satisfying the model's invariants. The using wp form works backward from the assertions to the conditions before construction.

Creation also preserves the three invariants. The new instance is outside the context, so it cannot duplicate the identity of a context member.

The uniqueness proof explicitly uses the fact that the four lifecycle states are distinct. The command have names that fact hd, and simp rewrites it into facts that grind can use.

With the individual proofs supplied, #check_invariants checks that the invariant obligations have been discharged.

#check_invariants

The command #gen_theorems assembles the checked results into theorems that the execution proofs in the next chapter can use.

#gen_theorems

The command #gen_executable generates executable versions of the same actions for finite model checks.

#gen_executable

We can now explore a small instance of the model. The Lean type Fin 3 contains the values 0, 1, and 2. We use these for three possible Java objects and three identity values. Reserving identity 0 for noIdentity leaves two actual persistent identities.

The command #model_check interpreted explores the reachable states of this finite instance and checks the model's properties. This is an executable check for these bounds; the proofs above apply without those bounds.

#model_check interpreted { entity := Fin 3, identity := Fin 3 } { noIdentity := 0 }

This completes the lifecycle module.

end EntityLifecycle

Guarantees for complete executions🔗

Formalized Specification

The lifecycle chapter proved that initialization establishes the three consistency conditions and that each operation preserves them. We now use those results to prove properties of entire executions: sequences of states connected by allowed operations.

We reopen the EntityLifecycle namespace so these theorems belong to the same model. The open commands make the library names and model notation available in the code below.

namespace EntityLifecycle open Veil Classical open scoped EntityLifecycle

The abbreviation Snapshot names the model's state type for entity type E and identity type I. An abbrev gives an existing expression a shorter name. The generated type phase_IndT represents our four lifecycle states.

abbrev Snapshot (E I : Type) := State (FieldAbstractType E I phase_IndT)

The abbreviation Background names the fixed information for an execution, including the chosen value of noIdentity. Veil calls this information the model's Theory.

abbrev Background (E I : Type) := Theory E I phase_IndT

The proofs use arbitrary entity and identity types. The square-bracketed requirements supply equality decisions (DecidableEq) and a default value (Inhabited) for each type. A default value also ensures the type is nonempty. No bound on the number of values is required.

variable {E I : Type} [DecidableEq E] [Inhabited E] [DecidableEq I] [Inhabited I]

The proposition Inv th s says that state s satisfies all three consistency conditions under background information th. The result type Prop means this is a statement to prove. Underscores in the expression let Lean infer arguments from their context.

abbrev Inv (th : Background E I) (s : Snapshot E I) : Prop := Invariants _ _ E I phase_IndT _ th s

The proposition Assumes th collects the model's assumptions. In our model, this requires an identity value other than noIdentity.

abbrev Assumes (th : Background E I) : Prop := Assumptions _ E I phase_IndT th

An execution is a function from natural numbers to snapshots: execution 0 is its initial state, and execution (n + 1) follows execution n. We define ELSpec to require initialization and, at each step, either an unchanged state or a transition described by one of the model's actions. Init and NextStep are the definitions generated from those actions.

This definition does not assume consistency; we will prove it. The noncomputable keyword allows us to use the logical transition definitions without requiring an algorithm to decide whether an infinite execution satisfies them.

noncomputable def ELSpec (th : Background E I) (execution : Nat → Snapshot E I) : Prop := Init _ _ E I phase_IndT _ th (execution 0) ∧ ∀ n, execution (n + 1) = execution n ∨ NextStep _ _ E I phase_IndT _ th (execution n) (execution (n + 1))

An execution may remain unchanged indefinitely. These theorems therefore do not promise that an operation eventually occurs. Database flush and transaction commit remain outside the model.

Our first theorem combines the three initialization proofs into Inv. The arguments ha and hi are proofs of the assumptions and initialization conditions. The tactic exact supplies the required proof; the angle brackets group the proofs of the three conditions together.

theorem InitialInvariant (th : Background E I) (s : Snapshot E I) (ha : Assumes th) (hi : Init _ _ E I phase_IndT _ th s) : Inv th s := E:TypeI:Typeinst✝³:DecidableEq Einst✝²:Inhabited Einst✝¹:DecidableEq Iinst✝:Inhabited Ith:Background E Is:Snapshot E Iha:Assumes thhi:Init (Background E I) (Snapshot E I) E I phase_IndT (FieldAbstractType E I phase_IndT) th s⊢ Inv th s All goals completed! 🐙

Merge preserves the source's lifecycle state and persistent identity. If the source is new or detached, it also returns a different Java object. In the statement below, s and t are the states before and after the call, and Merge.ext.tr is the transition relation generated from our action.

A created instance that is already detached remains detached after any allowed operation. In particular, merge creates or returns a managed target while leaving the detached source as it is. We first prove this for a single step. The proof considers each action and simplifies its transition definition.

We extend the single-step result to every adjacent pair of execution states. If the state is unchanged, the instance is still detached; otherwise, DetachedStep supplies the result for the operation that occurred.

The execution theorems are complete, so we close their namespace.

end EntityLifecycle

Finite regression checks🔗

Formalized Specification

The proofs cover arbitrary entity and identity types. We also execute the model with small finite types to check specific behaviors and compare them with the earlier TLA+ model. All transitions come from the actions defined in the lifecycle chapter.

We place the check definitions in the same namespace and make Veil's names and the model's notation available.

namespace EntityLifecycle open Veil open scoped EntityLifecycle

We use three possible Java objects, identified by 0, 1, and 2. The identity type has the same three values. FiniteState names the concrete state representation for these types; FiniteLabel names an operation together with its arguments, such as Persist 0 or Merge 0 1.

abbrev FiniteState := State (FieldConcreteType (Fin 3) (Fin 3) phase_IndT) abbrev FiniteLabel := Label (Fin 3) (Fin 3) phase_IndT

The fixed background information reserves identity 0 for noIdentity, leaving identities 1 and 2 available for persistent instances.

def finiteTheory : Theory (Fin 3) (Fin 3) phase_IndT := { noIdentity := 0 }

Veil's enumerableTransitionSystem supplies the initial states and the possible results of each action. We disable its routine logging and report the results of our checks below.

local instance : LogSwitch := ⟨false⟩ def finiteSystem := enumerableTransitionSystem (Fin 3) (Fin 3) phase_IndT finiteTheory

These three accessors read an instance's construction flag, lifecycle state, and persistent identity from the concrete state representation. Their longer bodies connect the checks to Veil's generated storage for those values.

def createdAt (s : FiniteState) (e : Fin 3) : Bool := (instFieldRepresentation (Fin 3) (Fin 3) phase_IndT .created).get s.created e def phaseAt (s : FiniteState) (e : Fin 3) : phase_IndT := (instFieldRepresentation (Fin 3) (Fin 3) phase_IndT .e_phase).get s.e_phase e def pidAt (s : FiniteState) (e : Fin 3) : Fin 3 := (instFieldRepresentation (Fin 3) (Fin 3) phase_IndT .pid).get s.pid e

For comparison with the saved results, we assign each lifecycle state a number. This encoding affects only how we record test results.

def phaseCode : phase_IndT → Nat | .new => 0 | .managed => 1 | .detached => 2 | .removed => 3

The function stateKey records all three objects in a fixed order. For each object it writes the construction flag, encoded lifecycle state, and identity. A semicolon separates one object's values from the next.

def stateKey (s : FiniteState) : String := String.intercalate ";" ([0, 1, 2].map fun (e : Fin 3) => s!"{if createdAt s e then 1 else 0},{phaseCode (phaseAt s e)},{(pidAt s e).val}")

The function labelKey gives each operation and its arguments a stable text representation. The scenario uses these names to select the prescribed call from the available transitions.

def labelKey : FiniteLabel → String | .Create e => s!"Create({e.val})" | .Persist e => s!"Persist({e.val})" | .Remove e => s!"Remove({e.val})" | .Refresh e => s!"Refresh({e.val})" | .Detach e => s!"Detach({e.val})" | .Merge e t => s!"Merge({e.val},{t.val})"

We list the three objects and define a Boolean check for context membership. It uses the same condition as belongsToContext: an instance has been created and is managed or removed. In executable Boolean expressions, && means “and,” || means “or,” and == tests equality.

def entities : List (Fin 3) := [0, 1, 2] def inContext (s : FiniteState) (e : Fin 3) : Bool := createdAt s e && (phaseAt s e == .managed || phaseAt s e == .removed)

The helper ensure stops a check with an error message when a condition is false. The type IO Unit describes an executable computation with effects, such as reporting an error, and no meaningful return value.

def ensure (ok : Bool) (message : String) : IO Unit := unless ok do throw (IO.userError message)

For each state, we check the three consistency conditions directly: new iff no identity, defaults for uncreated instances, and unique identities among context members. These executable assertions check the finite results; the general proofs remain in the preceding chapters.

def checkState (s : FiniteState) : IO Unit := do for e in entities do ensure ((phaseAt s e == .new) == (pidAt s e == 0)) "identity invariant" unless createdAt s e do ensure (phaseAt s e == .new && pidAt s e == 0) "uncreated defaults" for other in entities do if inContext s e && inContext s other && pidAt s e == pidAt s other then ensure (e == other) "unique context identity"

The function successors obtains every allowed next state from Veil's generated implementation. It checks each resulting state and confirms that detached instances stay detached. For merge, it checks that the source's attributes are preserved and that new or detached sources have distinct targets.

The remaining checks ensure that excluded calls never appear among successful transitions: merge on a removed instance, refresh on a nonmanaged instance, and persist or remove on a detached instance.

/-- Enumerate actual Veil actions, and check transition-level contracts and exclusions. -/ def successors (s : FiniteState) : IO (List (FiniteLabel × FiniteState)) := do let out := finiteSystem.tr finiteTheory s ensure out.failures.isEmpty "Veil assertion failure" for (label, t) in out.successes do checkState t for e in entities do if createdAt s e && phaseAt s e == .detached then ensure (phaseAt t e == .detached) "detached preservation" match label with | .Merge e target => ensure (phaseAt t e == phaseAt s e && pidAt t e == pidAt s e) "merge source attributes" if phaseAt s e == .new || phaseAt s e == .detached then ensure (target != e) "merge target distinctness" ensure (phaseAt s e != .removed) "removed merge excluded" if phaseAt s e == .managed then ensure (target == e) "managed merge target" | .Refresh e => ensure (phaseAt s e == .managed) "nonmanaged refresh excluded" | .Persist e | .Remove e => ensure (phaseAt s e != .detached) "detached call excluded" | _ => pure () return out.successes

TLC, the model checker used for the earlier TLA+ implementation, produced saved sets of states and transitions under verification/. The function compareFixture compares a newly computed set with the corresponding saved file and reports missing or extra entries. It compares the entries themselves, not just their counts.

def compareFixture (name : String) (actual : Std.HashSet String) : IO Unit := do let lines := (← IO.FS.readFile (s!"verification/{name}.txt")).splitOn "\n" let expected := Std.HashSet.ofList (lines.filter (! ·.isEmpty)) let missing := expected.toList.filter (!actual.contains ·) let extra := actual.toList.filter (!expected.contains ·) ensure (missing.isEmpty && extra.isEmpty) s!"{name}: {missing.length} missing, {extra.length} extra; first differences: {missing.take 3}, {extra.take 3}" IO.println s!"{name}: {actual.size} match the original TLC graph"

Starting from the single initial state, checkGraph explores every reachable state. It keeps a queue of states to visit and adds a successor only if it has not seen that state before. Each transition is recorded as a pair of state keys. Finally, both the states and the transitions are compared with the saved results. The 10,000-state guard is a resource limit for this check, not a restriction on the model's mathematical state space.

def checkGraph : IO Unit := do let mut queue := finiteSystem.initStates.toArray ensure (queue.size == 1) "exactly one initial state" let mut seen : Std.HashSet String := .ofList (queue.toList.map stateKey) let mut edges : Std.HashSet String := {} let mut index := 0 while index < queue.size do let s := queue[index]! checkState s for (_, t) in ← successors s do let key := stateKey t edges := edges.insert (stateKey s ++ ">" ++ key) unless seen.contains key do seen := seen.insert key queue := queue.push t ensure (queue.size ≤ 10000) "graph exceeded the regression check's resource limit" index := index + 1 compareFixture "lifecycle-states" seen compareFixture "lifecycle-edges" edges

The scenario follows 17 prescribed calls. Object 0 starts new; merging it creates managed object 1. Later, object 0 is persisted, removed, restored, and detached. Merging that detached source creates object 2 with the same identity. The final calls remove and then detach object 2. Repeated calls also exercise cases where an operation leaves the state unchanged.

/-- Exactly the original 17 prescribed operations, in order. -/ def scenario : List FiniteLabel := [ .Create 0, .Remove 0, .Detach 0, .Merge 0 1, .Merge 1 1, .Persist 0, .Persist 0, .Refresh 0, .Remove 0, .Remove 0, .Persist 0, .Detach 0, .Merge 0 2, .Merge 0 2, .Detach 0, .Remove 2, .Detach 2]

For each number of completed calls, expectedPhases lists the expected lifecycle states of objects 0, 1, and 2, in that order. Position zero describes the initial state, before any calls.

def expectedPhases (step : Nat) : List phase_IndT := if step ≤ 3 then [.new, .new, .new] else if step ≤ 5 then [.new, .managed, .new] else if step ≤ 8 then [.managed, .managed, .new] else if step ≤ 10 then [.removed, .managed, .new] else if step = 11 then [.managed, .managed, .new] else if step = 12 then [.detached, .managed, .new] else if step ≤ 15 then [.detached, .managed, .managed] else if step = 16 then [.detached, .managed, .removed] else [.detached, .managed, .detached]

After every call, we check those lifecycle states, which objects have been created, their identity relationships, and any pending removal. For example, after the thirteenth call, detached object 0 and managed object 2 must share an identity. The final checks also confirm that detached instances are outside the context.

def checkScenarioState (step : Nat) (s : FiniteState) : IO Unit := do ensure (step ≤ 17) "scenario step range" ensure (entities.map (phaseAt s) == expectedPhases step) s!"phases at step {step}" let expectedCreated : List (Fin 3) := if step = 0 then [] else if step ≤ 3 then [0] else if step ≤ 12 then [0, 1] else entities ensure (entities.filter (createdAt s) == expectedCreated) s!"created entities at step {step}" if step ≥ 6 then ensure (pidAt s 0 != pidAt s 1) "distinct allocated identities" if step ≥ 13 then ensure (pidAt s 0 == pidAt s 2) "detached copy identity" let pending := entities.filter fun e => createdAt s e && phaseAt s e == .removed let expectedPending : List (Fin 3) := if step = 9 || step = 10 then [0] else if step = 16 then [2] else [] ensure (pending == expectedPending) s!"pending removal at step {step}" if step ≥ 12 then ensure (!inContext s 0) "source outside context" if step = 17 then ensure (!inContext s 2) "second copy outside context"

The scenario driver keeps every state that can result from the calls so far, including both possible assignments of identities 1 and 2. For each state, the next prescribed call must have at least one successful result. A disabled call fails the check instead of silently ending that execution.

After all 17 calls, both identity assignments must reach the end. We compare the resulting states and transitions with the saved scenario, including the unchanged final step used by the earlier driver.

/-- Each prefix must enable the next prescribed call, for every identity choice. A disabled operation throws; it cannot make invariant checks pass vacuously. -/ def checkScenario : IO Unit := do ensure (scenario.length == 17) "scenario length" let mut frontier := finiteSystem.initStates let mut states : Std.HashSet String := {} let mut edges : Std.HashSet String := {} for s in frontier do checkScenarioState 0 s states := states.insert ("0|" ++ stateKey s) for (call, step) in scenario.zipIdx do let mut next := [] let mut keys : Std.HashSet String := {} for s in frontier do let selected := (← successors s).filter fun (label, _) => labelKey label == labelKey call ensure (!selected.isEmpty) s!"operation {step + 1} ({labelKey call}) disabled at {stateKey s}" for (_, t) in selected do checkScenarioState (step + 1) t let key := s!"{step + 1}|{stateKey t}" states := states.insert key edges := edges.insert (s!"{step}|{stateKey s}>" ++ key) unless keys.contains key do keys := keys.insert key next := t :: next frontier := next ensure (frontier.length == 2) "both identity assignments must finish" for s in frontier do -- The original driver explicitly stutters once it has finished. let key := "17|" ++ stateKey s edges := edges.insert (key ++ ">" ++ key) compareFixture "scenario-states" states compareFixture "scenario-edges" edges IO.println "All 17 operations reached for both identity assignments; all assertions and excluded calls checked."

The entry point runs the complete graph comparison and the scenario. Run it from the repository root with lake env lean --run Lifecycle/Checks.lean; any failed assertion makes the command fail.

def runChecks : IO Unit := do checkGraph checkScenario end EntityLifecycle def main : IO Unit := EntityLifecycle.runChecks

Proof trust audit🔗

Formalized Specification

The last check asks what assumptions our proofs depend on. An axiom is a statement accepted without a proof. We allow only three standard Lean axioms:

  • propext: logically equivalent propositions are equal.

  • Classical.choice: a value can be selected from any nonempty type.

  • Quot.sound: equivalent elements represent the same value in a quotient type, a type that treats those elements as equal.

The command run_cmd runs the following audit while Lean builds this chapter. It first checks that the three main results exist as theorems. It then visits every theorem in the EntityLifecycle namespace and uses collectAxioms to find its dependencies. Any axiom outside the allowed list fails the build through throwError.

This also rejects unfinished proofs and unchecked solver answers, which would introduce additional axioms. The executable checks in the previous chapter provide separate evidence about the finite model; they are not used as proofs of the general theorems.

open Lean in Audited 370 model theorems: only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound allowed.run_cmd do let allowed := [``propext, ``Classical.choice, ``Quot.sound] let required := [``EntityLifecycle.ELCorrect, ``EntityLifecycle.ELDetachedCorrect, ``EntityLifecycle.ELMergeSourceUnchanged] for name in required do unless (← getConstInfo name).isTheorem do throwError "Missing checked theorem: {name}" let mut count : Nat := 0 for (name, info) in (← getEnv).constants.toList do if (`EntityLifecycle).isPrefixOf name && info.isTheorem then count := count + 1 for axiomName in ← collectAxioms name do unless allowed.contains axiomName do throwError "Unapproved axiom in {name}: {axiomName}" logInfo m!"Audited {count} model theorems: only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound allowed."

We also print the axiom dependencies of the consistency theorem. The command #print axioms reports the axioms used by a theorem, including those used indirectly through other theorems.

'EntityLifecycle.ELCorrect' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]#print axioms EntityLifecycle.ELCorrect

The next command reports the dependencies of the theorem that a detached instance stays detached after each step.

'EntityLifecycle.ELDetachedCorrect' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]#print axioms EntityLifecycle.ELDetachedCorrect

Finally, we report the dependencies of the theorem that merge preserves its source's lifecycle state and identity and returns a distinct target for a new or detached source.

'EntityLifecycle.ELMergeSourceUnchanged' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]#print axioms EntityLifecycle.ELMergeSourceUnchanged

Open question🔗

What should merge(a) do when a is detached and another object with the same persistent identity is marked for removal? Suppose Book has no version or relationships, a book with ID 7L exists, and a transaction is active.

Book a = em.find(Book.class, 7L);
em.detach(a);
Book b = em.merge(a);  // a stays detached. b is managed.
em.remove(b);
Book c = em.merge(a);  // The argument is still a.

Two readings are plausible. The uniqueness rule in §3.6.10 suggests that b still occupies the identity and blocks creation of a copy. Read on its own, §3.6.9.2 calls for a new copy because there is no managed instance with that identity. To test the second reading, lake run failOnDuplicateIdentity applies the diff below to a temporary copy of the model's Merge action and runs Veil's finite model checker. The line is the condition for creating a fresh copy of the detached source e (here, a).

-      require ∀ other, belongsToContext other → pid other ≠ pid e
+      require ∀ other, e_phase other = managed → pid other ≠ pid e

The original line requires every object in the context to have a persistent identity different from a's. After remove(b), b still belongs to the context and has the same identity as a, so it blocks creation of c. This preserves uniqueness but leaves the outcome of the Java call open. The model specifies no successful merge for this case.

The replacement checks only objects whose lifecycle state is managed. It skips b because its state is removed. The final merge(a) can now create c, leaving two objects in the context with the same persistent identity. Veil reports the resulting violation of uniqueIdentity (§3.6.10).
